research_question: Why does pi have an infinite, non-repeating decimal expansion, and how is that fact different from calculating digits?

sources.title: Pi
sources.reliability: Mathematical reference maintained by Wolfram Research
notes: Pi is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter in Euclidean geometry.
Pi is irrational and has a non-terminating, non-repeating decimal expansion.
Pi occurs in many areas of mathematics beyond elementary circle measurements.

sources.title: Pi through the ages
sources.publisher: MacTutor History of Mathematics Archive, University of St Andrews
notes: Mathematicians have developed increasingly accurate approximations of pi over millennia.
Computing more digits is distinct from proving properties of the number itself.

sources.title: Rational and Irrational Numbers
notes: Rational numbers can be written as ratios of integers with nonzero denominators.
Rational decimals terminate or eventually repeat; irrational decimals do neither.

sources.title: Pi
notes: Pi has important uses in geometry and mathematical analysis.
Finite decimal values are approximations rather than the complete exact value.

sources.title: SI Units
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
notes: Measurement precision and uncertainty determine how many digits are useful in applied calculations.
